extracted.intended_audience: trial judges, litigators, law students, and others researching U.S. expert-evidence admissibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing the reliability and relevance of expert witness testimony under the U.S. Daubert standard, including the judicial 'gatekeeper' role, the factors courts consider, procedural challenges, and related case law applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial gatekeeping role
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial court judges must act as 'gatekeepers' to assess the reliability and relevance of expert witness testimony before it is presented to a jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges are required to assess the methodology and reasoning behind an expert's opinions, rather than simply relying on the expert's credentials or reputation. This is the overarching framework established by Daubert that transformed how courts evaluate expert evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testability of technique or theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technique or theory in question can be, and has been tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider empiricism and whether the method is subject to objective testing; lack of testability weighs against admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether it has been subjected to publication and peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer-reviewed publication supports reliability, though absence of publication is not necessarily dispositive; the factor helps evaluate acceptance and methodological scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known or potential error rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Its known or potential error rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine how often the technique produces incorrect results or how reliable its output is expected to be; a high or unquantified error rate can undermine admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards controlling operation
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence and maintenance of standards controlling its operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of established protocols, standardized procedures, and quality controls supports reliability; absence suggests the method may be insufficiently controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: General acceptance within relevant community
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether it has attracted widespread acceptance within a relevant scientific community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Daubert supplanted the Frye focus on general acceptance, community acceptance remains a relevant factor among others in assessing reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on methodology and reasoning (not credentials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial inquiry should focus on the expert's methodology and reasoning rather than merely the expert's credentials or reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expert's impressive qualifications do not replace an analysis of whether the methods used are scientifically valid and appropriately applied to the case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to non-scientific expert testimony (Kumho)
rubrics_metrics.description: Daubert may apply to non-scientific testimony, including testimony from engineers and other experts who are not scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael, the gatekeeping inquiry extends beyond strictly 'scientific' testimony to technical or specialized knowledge; courts must tailor the Daubert factors to the nature of the expert's discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review standard (Joiner)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellate court may review whether a trial court abused its discretion to admit or exclude expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under General Electric Co. v. Joiner, appellate courts evaluate admissibility rulings for abuse of discretion rather than de novo, which affects how trial courts exercise gatekeeping discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Rule of Evidence 702 as modified by Daubert
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Rule of Evidence 702 was modified based on Daubert and governs admissibility of expert testimony in federal courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daubert's principles are incorporated into Rule 702's requirement that expert testimony be both reliable and relevant; practitioners should analyze both the rule and the Daubert factors together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural mechanism to challenge admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposing counsel may bring a pretrial motion, including a motion in limine, to challenge expert testimony as inadmissible under Daubert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such motions are usually brought after the close of discovery with a hearing held prior to trial; timely procedural practice and evidentiary hearings are important to resolving admissibility disputes.
